claim: GABA modulates locomotory patterns in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: As a common neurotransmitter in the nervous system, γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) modulates locomotory patterns in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general statement about GABA's role.

claim: A GABAergic signal in C. elegans modulates the amplitude of undulatory head bending through extrasynaptic neurotransmission and conserved metabotropic receptors.
source: Here, we demonstrate that a GABAergic signal in C. elegans modulates the amplitude of undulatory head bending through extrasynaptic neurotransmission and conserved metabotropic receptors.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The GABAergic RME head motor neurons generate undulatory activity patterns that correlate with head bending.
source: We show that the GABAergic RME head motor neurons generate undulatory activity patterns that correlate with head bending and the activity of RME causally links with head bending amplitude.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: The activity of RME causally links with head bending amplitude.
source: We show that the GABAergic RME head motor neurons generate undulatory activity patterns that correlate with head bending and the activity of RME causally links with head bending amplitude.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by optogenetic experiments in Figure 6.

claim: The undulatory activity of RME is regulated by a pair of cholinergic head motor neurons SMD, which facilitate head bending.
source: The undulatory activity of RME is regulated by a pair of cholinergic head motor neurons SMD, which facilitate head bending, and inhibits SMD to limit head bending.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: RME inhibits SMD to limit head bending.
source: The undulatory activity of RME is regulated by a pair of cholinergic head motor neurons SMD, which facilitate head bending, and inhibits SMD to limit head bending.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The extrasynaptic neurotransmission between SMD and RME provides a gain control system to set head bending amplitude to a value correlated with optimal efficiency of forward movement.
source: The extrasynaptic neurotransmission between SMD and RME provides a gain control system to set head bending amplitude to a value correlated with optimal efficiency of forward movement.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: GABA plays a critical role in modulating locomotory patterns by regulating the underlying neural circuits at multiple levels.
source: Among a large number of neuromodulators, GABA, a major inhibitory neurotransmitter found in all nervous systems, plays a critical role in modulating locomotory patterns by regulating the underlying neural circuits at multiple levels (Tegner et al., 1993; Cazalets et al., 1998; Reith and Sillar, 1999; Swensen et al., 2000; Ziskind-Conhaim, 2013; Fidelin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In the crab Cancer borealis, GABA is identified in a few neuromodulatory neurons that project to the stomatogastric nervous system.
source: In the crab Cancer borealis, GABA is identified in a few neuromodulatory neurons that project to the stomatogastric nervous system, which generates a pyloric rhythmic pattern.
evidence: This is stated with reference to previous work.

claim: All the stomatogastric neurons respond to GABA with either an excitatory or inhibitory effect.
source: All the stomatogastric neurons respond to GABA with either an excitatory or inhibitory effect (Swensen et al., 2000), which are likely to contribute to the diverse motor patterns that can be generated by the stomatogastric system.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Swensen et al., 2000.

claim: In isolated lamprey spinal cord, an internally released GABA signal regulated spinal burst rate and modulated intersegmental coordination.
source: For example, in isolated lamprey spinal cord electrophysiological and pharmacological data showed that an internally released GABA signal regulated spinal burst rate and modulated intersegmental coordination (Tegner et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Tegner et al., 1993.

claim: In Xenopus laevis tadpoles, pharmacologically manipulating the activity of spinal GABAA receptor(s) alters the duration and rate of swimming episodes.
source: In Xenopus laevis tadpoles, pharmacologically manipulating the activity of spinal GABAA receptor(s) alters the duration and rate of swimming episodes (Reith and Sillar, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Reith and Sillar, 1999.

claim: In zebrafish larva, the activity of a set of GABA-producing sensory neurons in the spinal cord inhibits the slow fictive swimming events during either resting or active state.
source: In zebrafish larva, the activity of a set of GABA-producing sensory neurons in the spinal cord inhibits the slow fictive swimming events during either resting or active state (Fidelin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Fidelin et al., 2015.

claim: In the in vitro spinal cord preparation isolated from neonatal rats, GABA modulates the locomotory patterns.
source: In the in vitro spinal cord preparation isolated from neonatal rats, GABA modulates the locomotory patterns (Cazalets et al., 1998) and in the neonatal mouse spinal cord, GABAergic transmission is shown to play an integrated role in generating motor activity patterns (Ziskind-Conhaim, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Cazalets et al., 1998.

claim: In the neonatal mouse spinal cord, GABAergic transmission plays an integrated role in generating motor activity patterns.
source: In the in vitro spinal cord preparation isolated from neonatal rats, GABA modulates the locomotory patterns (Cazalets et al., 1998) and in the neonatal mouse spinal cord, GABAergic transmission is shown to play an integrated role in generating motor activity patterns (Ziskind-Conhaim, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Ziskind-Conhaim, 2013.

claim: GABAergic neurotransmission can act either synaptically through the ionic GABAA receptors or extrasynaptically through metabotropic GABAB receptors.
source: GABAergic neurotransmission can act either synaptically through the ionic GABAA receptors or extrasynaptically through metabotropic GABAB receptors (Dittman and Regehr, 1997; Isaacson et al., 1993; Sigel and Steinmann, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with references to previous work.

claim: The connectivity of the 302 neurons in a hermaphrodite adult C. elegans is well-defined.
source: The connectivity of the 302 neurons in a hermaphrodite adult C. elegans is well-defined (White et al., 1986), allowing identification of individual neurons and their connectivity with the rest of the nervous system.
evidence: This is stated with reference to White et al., 1986.

claim: Under the standard condition on a solid agar surface C. elegans generates forward undulatory movement that occurs at around 1 Hz bending oscillation on the dorsal-ventral plane.
source: Under the standard condition on a solid agar surface C. elegans generates forward undulatory movement that occurs at around 1 Hz bending oscillation on the dorsal-ventral plane.
evidence: This is a description of C. elegans locomotion behavior.

claim: The undulatory locomotory wave travels posteriorly from head to tail through contraction of body muscles.
source: The undulatory locomotory wave travels posteriorly from head to tail through contraction of body muscles (Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Wen et al., 2012.

claim: In an adult hermaphrodite, two major motor networks mediate forward movement, the head motor circuit and the ventral nerve cord motor circuit that innervate 95 muscle cells arranged in parallel rows along its dorsal and ventral sides.
source: In an adult hermaphrodite, two major motor networks mediate forward movement, the head motor circuit and the ventral nerve cord motor circuit that innervate 95 muscle cells arranged in parallel rows along its dorsal and ventral sides (Altun and Hall, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Altun and Hall, 2009.

claim: The head motor circuit that innervates the anterior muscle cells in the head and neck consists of several groups of excitatory cholinergic motor neurons, including four SMD neurons, and one group of inhibitory GABAergic motor neurons, the four RME neurons.
source: The head motor circuit that innervates the anterior muscle cells in the head and neck consists of several groups of excitatory cholinergic motor neurons, including four SMD (sublateral motor neurons class D) neurons, and one group of inhibitory GABAergic motor neurons, the four RME (ring motor neuron class E) neurons (Figure 1A, Altun and Hall, 2009; Gray et al., 2005; White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1A and previous work.

claim: The ventral nerve cord motor circuit that innervates the rest of the body wall muscles consists of excitatory cholinergic A-type and B-type motor neurons, which are required for backward and forward movement, respectively, as well as D-type GABAergic inhibitory motor neurons.
source: The ventral nerve cord motor circuit that innervates the rest of the body wall muscles consists of excitatory cholinergic A-type and B-type motor neurons, which are required for backward and forward movement, respectively, as well as D-type GABAergic inhibitory motor neurons (Chalfie et al., 1985; White et al., 1976; 1986).
evidence: This is stated with references to previous work.

claim: Both A- and B-type cholinergic neurons activate D-type GABAergic neurons that innervate the antagonistic muscles on the opposing side.
source: All ventral nerve cord motor neurons are subdivided into dorsal and ventral groups that innervate dorsal and ventral muscles, respectively; and both A- and B-type cholinergic neurons activate D-type GABAergic neurons that innervate the antagonistic muscles on the opposing side.
evidence: This describes the connectivity of the ventral nerve cord motor circuit.

claim: This network connectivity allows alternating contraction and relaxation of the dorsal and ventral muscles that propagates the undulatory body wave from the head region to the rest of the body during forward movements.
source: This network connectivity allows alternating contraction and relaxation of the dorsal and ventral muscles that propagates the undulatory body wave from the head region to the rest of the body during forward movements (Chalfie et al., 1985; Wen et al., 2012; White et al., 1976, 1986).
evidence: This is stated with references to previous work.

claim: Previous studies showed that disrupting biosynthesis of GABA altered the amplitude of undulatory head bending without disrupting forward movement.
source: Previous studies showed that disrupting biosynthesis of GABA altered the amplitude of undulatory head bending without disrupting forward movement (McIntire et al., 1993a; 1993b), suggesting that GABAergic neurotransmission is not required to generate forward undulatory body waves, but plays a modulatory role.
evidence: This is stated with references to McIntire et al., 1993a; 1993b.

claim: GABAergic neurotransmission is not required to generate forward undulatory body waves, but plays a modulatory role.
source: Previous studies showed that disrupting biosynthesis of GABA altered the amplitude of undulatory head bending without disrupting forward movement (McIntire et al., 1993a; 1993b), suggesting that GABAergic neurotransmission is not required to generate forward undulatory body waves, but plays a modulatory role.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that disrupting GABA biosynthesis alters but does not eliminate forward movement.

claim: Killing RME increased the amplitude of the undulatory head bending during forward movement.
source: However, killing RME increased the amplitude of the undulatory head bending during forward movement (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: The operated animals still made undulatory head bending and forward movement after killing RME neurons.
source: We found that the operated animals still made undulatory head bending and forward movement, suggesting that the RME GABAergic neurons are not required for the generation of the movements.
evidence: This is stated based on observations after laser ablation of RME neurons.

claim: The RME GABAergic neurons are not required for the generation of undulatory head bending and forward movement.
source: We found that the operated animals still made undulatory head bending and forward movement, suggesting that the RME GABAergic neurons are not required for the generation of the movements.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that animals still move after RME ablation.

claim: Killing the RMED/V pair increased head bending amplitude along the dorsal-ventral axis to the same extent as ablating all four RME neurons.
source: We found that killing the RMED/V pair increased head bending amplitude along the dorsal-ventral axis to the same extent as ablating all four RME neurons, whereas killing RMEL/R did not generate any obvious defect (Figure 1C and Videos 1, 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Killing RMEL/R did not generate any obvious defect in head bending amplitude.
source: We found that killing the RMED/V pair increased head bending amplitude along the dorsal-ventral axis to the same extent as ablating all four RME neurons, whereas killing RMEL/R did not generate any obvious defect (Figure 1C and Videos 1, 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: RMED/V neurons negatively regulate head bending amplitude.
source: Thus, RMED/V neurons negatively regulate head bending amplitude.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that killing RMED/V increases head bending amplitude.

claim: Both unc-25(e156) and unc-47(e307) mutants showed increased amplitude of head bending during forward movement.
source: Both unc-25(e156) and unc-47(e307) mutants showed increased amplitude of head bending during forward movement (Figure 1D and Videos 1, 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: The RME GABAergic neurons modulate forward movement by regulating the extent of the undulatory head bending.
source: Together, our results indicate that the RME GABAergic neurons modulate forward movement by regulating the extent of the undulatory head bending.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ablation and mutant experiments.

claim: RME generated undulatory calcium signals during head bending.
source: We found that RME generated undulatory calcium signals during head bending: RMED displayed increased intracellular calcium transients during dorsal head bending and RMEV displayed increased intracellular calcium transients during ventral head bending (Figure 1F,G and Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 1F and G.

claim: RMED displayed increased intracellular calcium transients during dorsal head bending.
source: We found that RME generated undulatory calcium signals during head bending: RMED displayed increased intracellular calcium transients during dorsal head bending and RMEV displayed increased intracellular calcium transients during ventral head bending (Figure 1F,G and Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 1G.

claim: RMEV displayed increased intracellular calcium transients during ventral head bending.
source: We found that RME generated undulatory calcium signals during head bending: RMED displayed increased intracellular calcium transients during dorsal head bending and RMEV displayed increased intracellular calcium transients during ventral head bending (Figure 1F,G and Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 1G.

claim: RMEV calcium activity positively correlated with head bending.
source: Using cross-correlation analysis, we found that RMEV calcium activity positively correlated with head bending and RMED calcium activity negatively correlated with head bending (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: RMED calcium activity negatively correlated with head bending.
source: Using cross-correlation analysis, we found that RMEV calcium activity positively correlated with head bending and RMED calcium activity negatively correlated with head bending (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: The calcium signals in RMEV and RMED were anti-correlated during head bending.
source: The calcium signals in RMEV and RMED were anti-correlated during head bending.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be inferred from Figure 1G and H.

claim: The oscillatory activity pattern allows RME to regulate head bending with a temporal pattern that matches that of head undulation.
source: The oscillatory activity pattern allows RME to regulate head bending with a temporal pattern that matches that of head undulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between RME activity and head bending.

claim: In animals immobilized with microbeads, RMED and REMV neurons generated oscillatory and anti-correlated calcium signals.
source: We found that in animals immobilized with microbeads (Kim et al., 2013) RMED and REMV neurons generated oscillatory and anti-correlated calcium signals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar calcium dynamics were observed in the RME neurons in the unc-54(e1092) null mutants.
source: In addition, we observed similar calcium dynamics in the RME neurons in the unc-54(e1092) null mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which lacked a major myosin heavy chain protein and were defective in muscle contraction (Dibb et al., 1985; MacLeod et al., 1977).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The undulatory calcium activity of the RME GABAergic neurons does not require head movement.
source: Therefore, the undulatory calcium activity of the RME GABAergic neurons does not require head movement.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations in immobilized animals and unc-54 mutants.

claim: In unc-13 mutant animals, the RME calcium activity did not correlate with head bending.
source: We found that the unc-13 mutant animals bent their heads in the microfluidic imaging device and generated active calcium transients in RME. However, the RME calcium activity in the unc-13 mutants did not correlate with head bending (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Blocking neuropeptide release in the unc-31(e928) mutants did not have an obvious effect on RME calcium activity.
source: In contrast, blocking neuropeptide release in the unc-31(e928) (Ann et al., 1997; Avery et al., 1993) mutants did not have an obvious effect on RME calcium activity (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Neurotransmitters, but not neuropeptides, regulate head bending-correlated calcium dynamics in RME.
source: These results indicate that neurotransmitters, but not neuropeptides, regulate head bending-correlated calcium dynamics in RME.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of unc-13 and unc-31 mutations.

claim: The hypomorphic allele cha-1(p1152) exhibited active calcium transients in RME that were not correlated with head bending.
source: We found that similar to the unc-13(e51) mutants the hypomorphic allele cha-1(p1152) (Rand and Russell, 1984) also exhibited active calcium transients in RME that were not correlated with head bending (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The defect in RME calcium activity in the cha-1(p1152) mutants was rescued by expressing the cosmid ZC416 that contained the genomic locus of cha-1.
source: The defect in RME calcium activity in the cha-1(p1152) mutants was rescued by expressing the cosmid ZC416 that contained the genomic locus of cha-1 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The head bending-correlated calcium activity in RME depends on cholinergic neurotransmission.
source: These results demonstrate that the head bending-correlated calcium activity in RME depends on cholinergic neurotransmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of cha-1 mutation and rescue.

claim: Restoring cha-1 expression in the SMB motor neurons or in the IL2 neurons could not rescue the defects in the head-bending correlated calcium activity in the RME neurons in the cha-1(p1152) mutant animals.
source: Surprisingly, we found that restoring cha-1 expression in the SMB motor neurons with the odr-2(18) promoter (Chou et al., 2001) or in the IL2 neurons with the klp-6 promoter (Lee et al., 2011; Peden and Barr, 2005) could not rescue the defects in the head-bending correlated calcium activity in the RME neurons in the cha-1(p1152) mutant animals (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The head bending-correlated calcium activity in RME may be independent of synaptic inputs.
source: These results suggest that the head bending-correlated calcium activity in RME may be independent of synaptic inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure of SMB and IL2-specific rescue to restore RME activity.

claim: SMDV and RMEV generated increased calcium transients during ventral head bending.
source: We found that SMDV and RMEV generated increased calcium transients during ventral head bending, while SMDD and RMED generated increased calcium transients during dorsal head bending (Figure 3A–C and Video 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: SMDD and RMED generated increased calcium transients during dorsal head bending.
source: We found that SMDV and RMEV generated increased calcium transients during ventral head bending, while SMDD and RMED generated increased calcium transients during dorsal head bending (Figure 3A–C and Video 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Expressing Pglr-1::cha-1 or Plad-2::cha-1 fully rescued the RME calcium dynamics that was correlated with dorsal-ventral head bending in cha-1(p1152) mutant animals.
source: Next, to address this hypothesis, we expressed the cha-1 cDNA under the glr-1 or the lad-2 promoter in the cha-1(p1152) mutant animals and found that either Pglr-1::cha-1 or Plad-2::cha-1 fully rescued the RME calcium dynamics that was correlated with dorsal-ventral head bending (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The only cholinergic head motor neurons that consistently express both the glr-1 and lad-2 promoters are SMD.
source: Both the glr-1 and lad-2 promoters drive expression in multiple cells, but the only cholinergic head motor neurons that consistently express both of the promoters are SMD (Brockie et al., 2001; Hendricks et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with references to previous work.

claim: Ablating SMD in the transgenic animals that expressed Pglr-1::cha-1 in the cha-1(p1152) mutant animals completely lost the rescuing effect on the RME calcium activity.
source: To strengthen the specificity of our results, we ablated SMD neurons in the transgenic animals that expressed Pglr-1::cha-1 in the cha-1(p1152) mutant animals. We found that the rescuing effect on the RME calcium activity was completely lost in the ablated animals (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3F and G.

claim: SMD plays an instructive role in generating the oscillatory calcium activity of RME.
source: Together, these results support the instructive role of SMD in generating the oscillatory calcium activity of RME.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue and ablation experiments.

claim: SMD neurons do not synapse onto RME.
source: Intriguingly, SMD neurons do not synapse onto RME (White et al., 1986), suggesting that extrasynaptic neurotransmission from SMD regulates RME.
evidence: This is stated with reference to the connectome from White et al., 1986.

claim: Extrasynaptic neurotransmission from SMD regulates RME.
source: Intriguingly, SMD neurons do not synapse onto RME (White et al., 1986), suggesting that extrasynaptic neurotransmission from SMD regulates RME.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of synaptic connections between SMD and RME.

claim: The head bending-correlated activity of RME was significantly reduced in the deletion mutant gar-2(ok520).
source: Interestingly, we found that the head bending-correlated activity of RME was significantly reduced in the deletion mutant gar-2(ok520) and the defect was fully rescued by expressing a wild-type gar-2 DNA fragment (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The defect in RME activity in gar-2(ok520) was fully rescued by expressing a wild-type gar-2 DNA fragment.
source: Interestingly, we found that the head bending-correlated activity of RME was significantly reduced in the deletion mutant gar-2(ok520) and the defect was fully rescued by expressing a wild-type gar-2 DNA fragment (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4A and B.

claim: GAR-2 mediates the SMD cholinergic signal to generate the undulatory activity pattern of RME.
source: This result indicates that GAR-2 mediates the SMD cholinergic signal to generate the undulatory activity pattern of RME.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of gar-2 mutation and rescue on RME activity.

claim: gar-2(ok520) displayed significantly larger amplitude of head bending.
source: Indeed, we found that gar-2(ok520) displayed significantly larger amplitude of head bending (Figure 4C and Video 6), similar to the effect of removing RMED and RMEV with laser ablation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Expressing a wild-type gar-2 cDNA with either the endogenous gar-2 promoter or the unc-25 promoter fully rescued the defect of the gar-2(ok520) mutants in head bending amplitude.
source: Expressing a wild-type gar-2 cDNA (Dittman and Kaplan, 2008) with either the endogenous gar-2 promoter or the unc-25 promoter that was selective for the GABAergic neurons (Jin et al., 1999) fully rescued the defect of the gar-2(ok520) mutants in head bending amplitude (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Among all GABAergic neurons only RME innervate head muscles and regulate head bending.
source: Among all GABAergic neurons only RME innervate head muscles and regulate head bending (Figure 1C) (McIntire et al., 1993b; White et al., 1976; 1986).
evidence: This is stated with references to previous work and data in Figure 1C.

claim: The extrasynaptic cholinergic neurotransmission of SMD facilitates the oscillatory activity of RME via the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor GAR-2 to regulate the amplitude of head bending.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that the extrasynaptic cholinergic neurotransmission of SMD facilitates the oscillatory activity of RME via the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor GAR-2 to regulate the amplitude of head bending.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments on SMD, RME, and GAR-2.

claim: Among all the neurons that consistently express the glr-1 promoter, only the cholinergic head neurons RMDD and RMDV are postsynaptic of SMD or connect with SMD via gap junction.
source: We found that among all the neurons that consistently express the glr-1 promoter, only the cholinergic head neurons RMDD and RMDV are postsynaptic of SMD or connect with SMD via gap junction.
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the connectome.

claim: Neither RMDD nor RMDV neurons synapse onto RME.
source: However, neither RMDD nor RMDV neurons synapse onto RME.
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the connectome.

claim: The head-bending correlated activity of RME is generated by extrasynaptic cholinergic neurotransmission that originates from the head motor neurons SMD.
source: Overall, our results in combination with the connectome reveal that the head-bending correlated activity of RME is generated by extrasynaptic cholinergic neurotransmission that originates from the head motor neurons SMD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments and connectome analysis.

claim: Blocking neurotransmission from SMD by expressing Tetanus Toxin with either the glr-1 or lad-2 promoter disrupted the head bending-correlated calcium dynamics in RME.
source: To further characterize the function of the SMD cholinergic neurons in driving RME calcium activity, we blocked the neurotransmission from SMD in wild-type animals by expressing Tetanus Toxin (TeTx) (Schiavo et al., 1992) with either the glr-1 or lad-2 promoter. We found that either mutation disrupted the head bending-correlated calcium dynamics in RME (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Blocking neurotransmission by expressing TeTx in SMB or IL2, or both SMB and IL2 had no effect on RME calcium activity.
source: However, blocking neurotransmission by expressing TeTx in two sets of major presynaptic neurons of RME, the cholinergic motor neurons SMB (Podr-2(18)::TeTx) or sensory neurons IL2 (Pklp-6::TeTx), or both SMB and IL2 had no effect on RME calcium activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that general reduction in cholinergic neurotransmission is not sufficient to disrupt RME calcium dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: General reduction in cholinergic neurotransmission is not sufficient to disrupt RME calcium dynamics.
source: However, blocking neurotransmission by expressing TeTx in two sets of major presynaptic neurons of RME, the cholinergic motor neurons SMB (Podr-2(18)::TeTx) or sensory neurons IL2 (Pklp-6::TeTx), or both SMB and IL2 had no effect on RME calcium activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that general reduction in cholinergic neurotransmission is not sufficient to disrupt RME calcium dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of blocking SMB and IL2 neurotransmission.

claim: Ablating SMD disrupted head bending-correlated calcium activities in RME while the RME neurons in the SMD-ablated animals remained active.
source: To address the question more specifically, we also performed laser ablation of SMD. We found that ablating SMD disrupted head bending-correlated calcium activities in RME while the RME neurons in the SMD-ablated animals remained active (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Ablating the IL2 sensory neurons had no effect on RME calcium activity.
source: In contrast, ablating the IL2 sensory neurons had no effect (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The cholinergic excitatory motor neurons SMD drive the head bending-correlated oscillatory activity in RME through an extrasynaptic signal.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that the cholinergic excitatory motor neurons SMD drive the head bending-correlated oscillatory activity in RME through an extrasynaptic signal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TeTx and ablation experiments.

claim: RME generates a modulatory signal that limits head bending amplitude.
source: RME generates a modulatory signal that limits head bending amplitude.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of RME ablation and manipulation.

claim: The oscillatory activity of RME provides a mechanism through which the GABAergic modulatory signal mediates head bending with a temporal pattern that matches that of head undulation.
source: The oscillatory activity of RME provides a mechanism through which the GABAergic modulatory signal mediates head bending with a temporal pattern that matches that of head undulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between RME activity and head bending.

claim: The deletion mutation in gbb-1(tm1406) increased the amplitude of head bending during forward movement.
source: We found that similar to removing the GABA biosynthetic enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase in the unc-25(e156) null mutant animals, the deletion mutation in gbb-1(tm1406) increased the amplitude of head bending during forward movement (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: The double mutant gbb-1(tm1406);gbb-2(tm1165) similarly increased head bending amplitude.
source: In addition, the double mutant gbb-1(tm1406);gbb-2(tm1165) similarly increased head bending amplitude (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with the notion that GBB-1 and GBB-2 function as heterodimers (Dittman and Kaplan, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: GBB-1 and GBB-2 function as heterodimers.
source: In addition, the double mutant gbb-1(tm1406);gbb-2(tm1165) similarly increased head bending amplitude (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with the notion that GBB-1 and GBB-2 function as heterodimers (Dittman and Kaplan, 2008).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Dittman and Kaplan, 2008.

claim: The exaggerated head bending in the gbb-1(tm1406) mutant animals was rescued by expressing a wild-type gbb-1 cDNA under the gbb-1 endogenous promoter.
source: The exaggerated head bending in the gbb-1(tm1406) mutant animals was rescued by expressing a wild-type gbb-1 cDNA under the gbb-1 endogenous promoter (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: The GABAB receptor GBB-1/GBB-2 restrains the head bending amplitude.
source: Thus, similar to the RMED/V neurons (Figure 1C), the GABAB receptor GBB-1/GBB-2 restrains the head bending amplitude.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of gbb-1 mutation and rescue.

claim: The transcriptional reporter of gbb-1 was expressed in a number of head neurons, including SMD.

claim: In the case of slender organisms undulating in Newtonian fluids, the classical resistance force theory predicts quantitatively that the propulsion efficiency grows with the angle of attack.
source: In the case of slender organisms undulating in Newtonian fluids, the classical resistance force theory (Gray and Hancock, 1955) predicts quantitatively that the propulsion efficiency, which is defined as the ratio of the actual speed (Va) to the wave speed of body undulation (Vw) in the reference frame of a worm, grows with the angle of attack (θa), which is defined as the mean angle of a body segment with respect to the direction of forward movement (Fang-Yen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with references to Gray and Hancock, 1955 and Fang-Yen et al., 2010.

claim: Experimental data closely fit the theoretical curve relating propulsion efficiency to angle of attack.
source: Using wild-type animals we measured both variables during bouts of (~10–15 s) forward locomotion (The data points in Figure 7A), and found that experimental data closely fit the theoretical curve (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7A.
